extracted.intended_audience: school teachers (especially new or early-career classroom instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for running a schoolroom: establishing moral authority, first impressions, correcting faults, and engaging pupils in collective reforms rather than humiliating or punishing individuals. Emphasizes methods, tone, and concrete techniques for mass discipline and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to the whole school; elevate the mass
rubrics_metrics.description: The school, the whole school, is your field; the elevation of the mass in knowledge and virtue is your duty, and no individual instance of dulness or precocity should draw you away from its steady pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not devote a disproportionate degree of attention to single pupils (whether dull or precocious). Your aim should be broad improvement across the whole pupil body rather than focusing on isolated cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against faulty mental habits acquired from the station
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers are in danger of imbibing narrowminded prejudices, prepossessions, and an excessive confidence in their own views because they rarely hear their opinions contradicted in the school-room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-aware: avoid insisting that 'your way' in minute particulars is the only tolerable way; welcome dissent and avoid developing arrogance or rigid formalism in methods (e.g., obsessing over whether an 'o' is pointed or round).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid set, formal mannerism; cultivate boldness and enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Set, formal mannerism is inconsistent with the commanding intellectual influence a teacher should exert; activity and enterprise of mind should characterize all measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with 'boldness and freedom of touch'—be creative, original, and energetic in methods rather than mechanically adhering to ritualized forms of behaviour or instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume no false appearances; admit ignorance honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pretend superior knowledge, infallibility, or a forced dignity; if a scholar asks a question you cannot answer, say frankly, 'I do not know.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealing ignorance (e.g., giving evasive general directions or stalling) is dishonest and counterproductive. Honesty secures real respect; you may position yourself as guide by virtue of maturity and method even when learning alongside pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a good first impression; greet pupils warmly
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of making an unfavorable first impression upon your pupils; meet them with a smile and a genuine interest rather than a stern, forbidding manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A harsh first greeting can remain the only remembered act of a teacher for a lifetime. Avoid forced gravity and affectation—show sincere interest, 'shut your eyes for a day or two to their faults,' and present an alluring initial attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct classes of faults with general measures, not isolated punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: In correcting faults, do not seize only upon particular transgressions that come under your notice; instead ascertain whether a fault prevails generally and devise plans to reach the whole evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than calling and punishing the accidentally observed offender, address the whole school about the issue, diagnose prevalence, and implement school-wide corrective measures that target the root problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use calm moral appeal instead of scolding and anger
rubrics_metrics.description: A calm, temperate address explaining the nature of a fault and inviting voluntary confession and reform is more effective than scolding, storming, and punishment driven by irritation and anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: upon overhearing profane language, the teacher delays, then addresses the class in a calm way—explaining wrong, inviting those willing to reform to rise, offering help and a plan—rather than publicly punishing an individual. Habitual scolders will not gain trust; temper and consistency matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blunting conscience when avoiding anger
rubrics_metrics.description: While avoiding tones of irritation is important, be cautious not to speak so lightly of a fault that you blunt the pupil's sense of its guilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is required: speak calmly and temperately but preserve clear moral seriousness so that reform is not trivialized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest pupils in reforms; enlist a decided cooperating majority
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest your scholars in doing something themselves to elevate the moral character of the school so as to secure a decided majority who will co-operate of their own accord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't merely command improvements—present plans as shared projects, invite votes, nominations, and voluntary commitments so pupils take ownership and pride in the institution's betterment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame reforms as moral experiments with measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Present improvement plans as experiments whose commencement, progress, and results pupils can observe—record baseline data and re-examine to see progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: record the number of disorderly desks on a date, appoint a monitor to keep the record, predict outcomes with the class, re-count after a period to measure improvement. Use committee selection, recorded targets, and follow-ups to make reforms engaging and empirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer general measures over public exposure for minor faults (desk example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of publicly reproving a single student's disorderly desk, address the whole class about desk order, define what 'good order' means, give time for correction, and follow up with inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public shaming produces sullen reactions and superficial fixes; a general classroom lesson with explicit principles, a brief work period, and a planned re-examination accomplishes far more, with less irritation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe discreetly and build on small approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: When disorder appears, 'observe' rather than immediately punish—study the materials and movements, find something to approve, and use that as leverage to interest the class in reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch 'without seeming to watch', let character reveal itself, intersperse a relevant anecdote or explanation to engage pupils during exercises, and close by directing their attention to desirable behaviour rather than merely reproving faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate pride and positive expectations rather than mere satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not act as if correct behavior is merely to be expected and not worth notice; pupils should share in the pleasure of improvement and receive acknowledgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make improvements a source of shared positive feeling; when students do right, notice and celebrate it—this provides motivation beyond fear of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the teacher's tone and manner as a primary instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of plans for moral discipline depends less on precise methods than on the teacher's own view of them and the tone and manner in which the teacher addresses pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language, demeanor, and consistency determine whether appeals will be taken seriously. Adjust phrasing to encourage cooperation rather than provoke resistance.
